claim: Smooth interfaces form between expanding Arp2/3-based actin caps and surrounding actomyosin networks across the syncytial Drosophila embryo surface.
source: Across the syncytial Drosophila embryo surface, smooth interfaces form between expanding Arp2/3-based actin caps and surrounding actomyosin networks, demarcating the circumferences of nascent dome-like compartments used for pseudocleavage.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Forming a smooth and circular boundary of the surrounding actomyosin domain requires Arp2/3 in vivo.
source: We found that forming a smooth and circular boundary of the surrounding actomyosin domain requires Arp2/3 in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Arp3 RNAi experiments shown in Figure 3A, where depletion of Arp3 resulted in rough boundaries.

claim: In simulations of actomyosin networks with local clearances in place of Arp2/3 domains, rough boundaries persisted when myosin contractility was low.
source: In simulations of actomyosin networks with local clearances in place of Arp2/3 domains, rough boundaries persisted when myosin contractility was low.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 3C-D and Figure 4A.

claim: With addition of expanding Arp2/3 network domains, myosin domain boundaries failed to smoothen, but accumulated myosin nodes and tension.
source: With addition of expanding Arp2/3 network domains, myosin domain boundaries failed to smoothen, but accumulated myosin nodes and tension.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 4A-B demonstrating myosin node accumulation and increased tension at interfaces.

claim: After incorporating actomyosin mechanosensitivity, Arp2/3 network growth locally induced a surrounding contractile actomyosin ring that smoothened the interface between the cytoskeletal domains.
source: After incorporating actomyosin mechanosensitivity, Arp2/3 network growth locally induced a surrounding contractile actomyosin ring that smoothened the interface between the cytoskeletal domains, an effect also evident in vivo.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data in Figure 4C-D and Figure 5, and supported by in vivo observations in Figure 3A.

claim: Tubulin subunits assemble microtubules with relatively high rigidity, allowing microtubules to act as smooth tracks for molecular transport through the cell.
source: For example, tubulin subunits assemble microtubules with relatively high rigidity, allowing microtubules to act as smooth tracks for molecular transport through the cell (Hawkins et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hawkins et al., 2010.

claim: Individual actin polymers have lower rigidity than microtubules.
source: Individual actin polymers have lower rigidity (Salbreux et al., 2012), but cross-linking by actin-binding proteins can bundle multiple polymers into straight structures that support cell protrusions (Svitkina, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Salbreux et al., 2012 and Svitkina, 2018.

claim: Cross-linking by actin-binding proteins can bundle multiple actin polymers into straight structures that support cell protrusions.
source: Individual actin polymers have lower rigidity (Salbreux et al., 2012), but cross-linking by actin-binding proteins can bundle multiple polymers into straight structures that support cell protrusions (Svitkina, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Svitkina, 2018.

claim: In the Drosophila wing imaginal disc, non-muscle myosin II is required to pull actin networks into straight cables integrated via cell-cell junctions to form smooth compartment boundaries.
source: In the Drosophila wing imaginal disc, gene expression patterns define the cells of specific compartments, but non-muscle myosin II (myosin hereafter) is then required to pull actin networks into straight cables integrated via cell-cell junctions to form smooth compartment boundaries that define the architecture of the mature wing (Harris, 2018; Wang and Dahmann, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Harris, 2018 and Wang and Dahmann, 2020.

claim: During mesenchymal cell migration, a leader cell's initial path through the extracellular matrix is smoothened by follower cells through reciprocal mechanical effects that co-align cellular actomyosin cables with extracellular matrix fibers via focal adhesions.
source: Another example comes from mesenchymal cell migration. Here, a leader cell's initial path through the extracellular matrix is smoothened by follower cells as reciprocal mechanical effects co-align cellular actomyosin cables with extracellular matrix fibers via focal adhesions (Livne and Geiger, 2016; van Helvert et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Livne and Geiger, 2016 and van Helvert et al., 2018.

claim: During cytokinesis, spindle-derived cues roughly organize actomyosin assemblies around the cell equator, and myosin activity then contributes to smoothening of the contractile cytokinetic ring.
source: A purely subcellular example occurs during cytokinesis, when spindle-derived cues roughly organize actomyosin assemblies around the cell equator, and myosin activity then contributes to smoothening of the contractile cytokinetic ring that divides the cell in two (Schwayer et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schwayer et al., 2016.

claim: The cell cortex is a thin, sheet-like material underlying the cell's plasma membrane.
source: In addition to specialized structures, such as junction-associated cables or cytokinetic rings, actin networks also form the cell cortex, a thin, sheet-like material underlying the cell's plasma membrane (Chugh and Paluch, 2018; Svitkina, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chugh and Paluch, 2018 and Svitkina, 2020.

claim: Cortical asymmetry can elicit cortical flow, with resulting compressive forces promoting mesoscale alignment of actin filaments perpendicular to the flow.
source: Cortical asymmetry can elicit cortical flow (Munro, 2006), with resulting compressive forces promoting mesoscale alignment of actin filaments perpendicular to the flow (Reymann et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Munro, 2006 and Reymann et al., 2016.

claim: The cortex's composite structure involves distinct actin-based networks: formin-induced networks, with or without myosin, and Arp2/3-induced networks.
source: The cortex's composite structure involves distinct actin-based networks: formin-induced networks, with or without myosin, and Arp2/3-induced networks (Chugh and Paluch, 2018; Svitkina, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chugh and Paluch, 2018 and Svitkina, 2020.

claim: The budding of a polar body from an oocyte involves induction of an Arp2/3-enriched domain surrounded by a smooth ring of actomyosin.
source: For example, the budding of a polar body from a much larger oocyte involves induction of an Arp2/3-enriched domain surrounded by a smooth ring of actomyosin (Yi and Li, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yi and Li, 2012.

claim: The Arp2/3-enriched domain prevents full contraction of the actomyosin ring during polar body budding.
source: The Arp2/3-enriched domain prevents full contraction of the actomyosin ring, and the actomyosin ring delineates the boundary of budding polar body, but how a smooth interface forms between such networks remains unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yi and Li, 2012 in the preceding sentence.

claim: Centrosomes provide local spatial cues that induce an Arp2/3-enriched actin cap above each nucleus in the early Drosophila embryo.
source: Centrosomes provide local spatial cues that induce an Arp2/3-enriched actin cap above each nucleus (Foe et al., 2000; Raff and Glover, 1989; Stevenson et al., 2002; Stevenson et al., 2001; Zallen et al., 2002), and each cap is surrounded by an actomyosin border (Foe et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Foe et al., 2000; Raff and Glover, 1989; Stevenson et al., 2002; Stevenson et al., 2001; Zallen et al., 2002.

claim: Each actin cap in the early Drosophila embryo is surrounded by an actomyosin border.
source: Centrosomes provide local spatial cues that induce an Arp2/3-enriched actin cap above each nucleus (Foe et al., 2000; Raff and Glover, 1989; Stevenson et al., 2002; Stevenson et al., 2001; Zallen et al., 2002), and each cap is surrounded by an actomyosin border (Foe et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Foe et al., 2000.

claim: At the onset of each synchronous mitotic cycle in the early Drosophila embryo, the caps and borders assemble anew and expand as cortical domains with rough boundaries.
source: At the onset of each synchronous mitotic cycle, the caps and borders assemble anew, and expand as cortical domains with rough boundaries (Foe et al., 2000; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Foe et al., 2000 and Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: As the caps and borders meet, they form a smooth, circular interface that demarcates the circumference of a nascent dome-like compartment.
source: As the caps and borders meet, they form a smooth, circular interface that demarcates the circumference of a nascent dome-like compartment.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by in vivo imaging data in Figure 3A.

claim: Initial assembly of each cortical domain in the early Drosophila embryo is induced by signaling of distinct small G proteins.
source: Initial assembly of each domain is induced by signaling of distinct small G proteins (Blake-Hedges and Megraw, 2019; Lv et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Blake-Hedges and Megraw, 2019 and Lv et al., 2021.

claim: With experimental depletion of one network, the other network expands its domain laterally due to an apparent loss of physical restriction.
source: For example, with experimental depletion of one network, the other network expands its domain laterally due to an apparent loss of physical restriction (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: The Arp2/3 network is necessary for compartment formation in the early Drosophila embryo.
source: The Arp2/3 network is necessary for compartment formation (Stevenson et al., 2002; Zallen et al., 2002), and when myosin levels or activity are experimentally reduced, growth and buckling of the actin cap appears sufficient to form a compartment (Royou et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Stevenson et al., 2002 and Zallen et al., 2002.

claim: When myosin levels or activity are experimentally reduced, growth and buckling of the actin cap appears sufficient to form a compartment.
source: The Arp2/3 network is necessary for compartment formation (Stevenson et al., 2002; Zallen et al., 2002), and when myosin levels or activity are experimentally reduced, growth and buckling of the actin cap appears sufficient to form a compartment (Royou et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Royou et al., 2004 and Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: With myosin depletion, the actin cap grows with an irregular shape, and the dome-like compartment is abnormally lop-sided.
source: With myosin depletion, however, the actin cap grows with an irregular shape, and the dome-like compartment is abnormally lop-sided (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: The simulated actomyosin network mimics mesoscale properties of actomyosin networks reconstituted in vitro.
source: The actomyosin network model mimics properties of actomyosin networks reported in vitro
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing simulation results in Figure 1B-E with in vitro studies by Schuppler et al., 2016 and in vivo studies by Izquierdo et al., 2018.

claim: In vitro, inducing myosin motor activity in specific geometric patterns within a larger non-contractile network shows that re-shaping of the embedded contractile actomyosin network is influenced by the boundary pattern of its initial activation.
source: By inducing myosin motor activity in specific geometric patterns within a larger non-contractile network in vitro, Schuppler et al., 2016 showed that re-shaping of the embedded contractile actomyosin network is influenced by the boundary pattern of its initial activation (Schuppler et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schuppler et al., 2016.

claim: An activated circle of actomyosin contracted into a smaller circle in vitro.
source: As a simple example, an activated circle of actomyosin contracted into a smaller circle.
evidence: This is stated in reference to Schuppler et al., 2016 in vitro studies.

claim: The edges of an activated square of actomyosin became concave in vitro.
source: More interestingly, the edges of an activated square became concave, whereas the edges of an activated outline of a square became convex (Schuppler et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schuppler et al., 2016.

claim: The edges of an activated outline of a square of actomyosin became convex in vitro.
source: More interestingly, the edges of an activated square became concave, whereas the edges of an activated outline of a square became convex (Schuppler et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schuppler et al., 2016.

claim: Optogenetic activation of actomyosin in the Drosophila embryo ectoderm resulted in the edges of an activated square becoming concave as the square contracted.
source: Remarkably, optogenetic activation of actomyosin in the complex environment of the Drosophila embryo ectoderm had a similar effect: the edges of an activated square became concave as the square contracted (Izquierdo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Izquierdo et al., 2018.

claim: In simulations, an activated circle of myosin nodes displayed isotropic contraction.
source: Not surprisingly, an activated circle displayed isotropic contraction (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In simulations, the sides of an activated solid square of myosin nodes became concave.
source: Notably, the sides of an activated solid square became concave (Figure 1C), mimicking both the in vitro (Schuppler et al., 2016) and in vivo studies (Izquierdo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 1C and matches in vitro and in vivo observations.

claim: In simulations, the outer sides of a hollow square with a thin boundary of activation became convex.
source: The outer sides of a hollow square with a thin boundary of activation became convex (Figure 1D), mimicking the in vitro behavior (Schuppler et al., 2016).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 1D and matches in vitro observations.

claim: For a hollow square with a thick boundary of activation, the outer sides of the boundary became concave and the inner edges bent in the opposite direction in simulations.
source: For a hollow square with a thick boundary of activation, the outer sides of the boundary became concave and the inner edges bent in the opposite direction (Figure 1E), as also seen in vitro (Schuppler et al., 2016).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 1E and matches in vitro observations.

claim: When simulated individually, a centrally induced Arp2/3 network grows centrifugally with an outer perimeter of non-aligned actin plus end nodes.
source: When simulated individually, a centrally induced Arp2/3 network grows centrifugally with an outer perimeter of non-aligned actin plus end nodes (Figure 1G), a behavior resembling initial in vivo growth of an actin cap in the embryo surface plane (e.g. Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 1G and compared to in vivo observations.

claim: Arp2/3 network growth against a cantilever leads to an increased density of F-actin plus ends at the interface, without an accumulation of elastic energy in vitro.
source: By combining light and atomic force microscopy, Bieling et al., 2016 found that Arp2/3 network growth against a cantilever lead to an increased density of F-actin plus ends at the interface, without an accumulation of elastic energy (Bieling et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bieling et al., 2016.

claim: In simulations, with Arp2/3 network growth into an immovable wall, the density of plus end nodes within 20 pixels of the network circumference increased 1.57-fold from the start of the simulation to step 3000.
source: With network growth into the immovable wall, the density of plus end nodes within 20 pixels of the network circumference increased 1.57-fold from the start of the simulation to step 3000 (calculated from four simulations with distinct starting conditions; see images in Figure 1H).
evidence: This is calculated from simulation data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: For simulated Arp2/3 networks growing without a wall, the density of plus end nodes within 20 pixels of the network circumference decreased 0.77-fold by simulation step 3000.
source: For networks growing without a wall, the equivalent value decreased 0.77-fold by simulation step 3000 (see example images in Figure 1G).
evidence: This is calculated from simulation data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: In simulations, network area growth rates after removal of the wall were indistinguishable from those of networks that never experienced a wall.
source: However, network area growth rates after removal of the wall were indistinguishable from those of networks that never experienced a wall (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: In simulations, a broad ring of myosin nodes with zero myosin activity maintained its structure.
source: Without myosin activity (0.0), the broad ring maintained its structure (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In simulations, with full myosin activity (1.0), a broad ring of dispersed nodes initially constricted into a narrow ring of nodes, and after thinning, the ring constricted centripetally.
source: With full myosin activity (1.0), the broad ring of dispersed nodes initially constricted into a narrow ring of nodes, and after thinning, the ring constricted centripetally (Figure 2E), a sequence of events consistent with in vitro observations of a myosin network activated in a rectangular shape (Schuppler et al., 2016).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 2E and compared to in vitro observations.

claim: In simulations, adding a growing Arp2/3 network to the center of a broad ring with zero or moderate myosin activity led to centrifugal displacement of myosin nodes and a thinning of the ring, but no ring constriction was observed.
source: Adding a growing Arp2/3 network to the center of a broad ring with zero or moderate myosin activity led to centrifugal displacement of myosin nodes and a thinning of the ring, but no ring constriction was observed (Figure 2B,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 2B and 2D.

claim: In simulations, as the Arp2/3 network grew, the thinned ring of myosin nodes was displaced outward and displayed diminished circularity that resembled the rough outer edge of the segregated Arp2/3 network.
source: As the Arp2/3 network grew, the thinned ring of myosin nodes was displaced outward and displayed diminished circularity that resembled the rough outer edge of the segregated Arp2/3 network.
evidence: This is observed in simulation data shown in Figure 2B and 2D.

claim: In simulations, during displacement by Arp2/3 network growth, the two networks remained segregated and myosin nodes aggregated at the network-network interface.
source: During this displacement, the two networks remained segregated, confirming the effectiveness of the node-based rules, and myosin nodes aggregated at the network-network interface (Figure 2B,D, arrows).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 2B and 2D.

claim: In simulations, with full myosin node activity, the actomyosin ring counteracted the expansion of the central Arp2/3 network.
source: With full myosin node activity, the actomyosin ring counteracted the expansion of the central Arp2/3 network (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: In control RNAi embryos during the transition from mitotic cycle 10 to 11, the actomyosin network initially assembled a rough, non-circular interface around each myosin-devoid cap, but within minutes, smooth and circular boundaries formed.
source: In control RNAi embryos during the transition from mitotic cycle 10 to 11, the actomyosin network initially assembled a rough, non-circular interface around each myosin-devoid cap, but within minutes, smooth and circular boundaries formed (Figure 3A; the transition was most obvious for completely new networks formed between sister nuclei, solid black arrows).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In Arp3 RNAi embryos, actomyosin networks failed to form smooth boundaries and instead retained a variable distribution of puncta at the interface with the myosin-devoid cap.
source: In contrast, Arp3 RNAi embryos assembled actomyosin networks that failed to form smooth boundaries and instead retained a variable distribution of puncta at the interface with the myosin-devoid cap (Figure 3A, solid red arrows).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In control embryos, the formation of a smooth interface was often accompanied by an accumulation of Zip-GFP along the interface.
source: In control embryos, the formation of a smooth interface was often accompanied by an accumulation of Zip-GFP along the interface (Figure 3A, solid and hollow black arrows), and both demarked the site of initial pseudo-cleavage furrow ingression (Figure 3A, 143s, side view, blue arrowheads).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Arp3 RNAi embryos lacked Zip-GFP accumulation at the interface and furrow ingression failed.
source: Arp3 RNAi embryos lacked Zip-GFP accumulation at the interface (Figure 3A, solid and hollow red arrows) and furrow ingression failed (Figure 3A, 143s, side view, blue bracket shows a broad band of myosin at the embryo surface).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The Arp2/3-based actin network of the cap is required for forming a smooth interface with the actomyosin border.
source: These data suggest that the Arp2/3-based actin network of the cap is required for forming a smooth interface with the actomyosin border, and that smooth interface formation coincides with myosin accumulation and furrow initiation at the interface.
evidence: This is inferred from in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 3A comparing control and Arp3 RNAi embryos.

claim: Smooth interface formation coincides with myosin accumulation and furrow initiation at the interface.
source: These data suggest that the Arp2/3-based actin network of the cap is required for forming a smooth interface with the actomyosin border, and that smooth interface formation coincides with myosin accumulation and furrow initiation at the interface.
evidence: This is observed in in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Both actomyosin and Arp2/3 networks initially have a rough boundary.
source: Notably, both networks initially have a rough boundary (Zhang et al., 2018; Figure 3A), and the smooth interface seems to arise from their lateral interaction.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2018 and in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The smooth interface seems to arise from the lateral interaction of the actomyosin and Arp2/3 networks.
source: Notably, both networks initially have a rough boundary (Zhang et al., 2018; Figure 3A), and the smooth interface seems to arise from their lateral interaction.
evidence: This is inferred from in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 3A and simulation results.

claim: In simulations without Arp2/3 networks, at node densities that retained connectivity (0.1–0.25), higher myosin activities (0.2–1.0) produced smooth and circular boundaries with the clearances.
source: At node densities that retained connectivity (0.1–0.25), higher myosin activities (0.2–1.0) produced smooth and circular boundaries with the clearances (Figure 3C, yellow arrows).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: High myosin activity is sufficient to produce extended, smooth structures in vivo, such as cell junction-associated actomyosin cables or the cytokinetic ring.
source: This result is consistent with the sufficiency of myosin activity to produce extended, smooth structures in vivo, such as cell junction-associated actomyosin cables (Harris, 2018; Livne and Geiger, 2016) or the cytokinetic ring (Schwayer et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Harris, 2018; Livne and Geiger, 2016; and Schwayer et al., 2016.

claim: In simulations without Arp2/3 networks, low myosin activity (0.1) allowed persistence of rough boundaries with the clearances.
source: In contrast, low myosin activity (0.1) allowed persistence of rough boundaries with the clearances (Figure 3C; red arrows), and displayed modest network rearrangements during early stages of the simulation (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: The simulated myosin distribution with low activity and rough boundaries resembled the myosin distribution in Arp3 RNAi embryos.
source: This result resembled the myosin distribution in Arp3 RNAi embryos (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is concluded by comparing simulation data in Figure 3C-D with in vivo data in Figure 3A.

claim: Myosin activity is relatively low in the early Drosophila embryo.
source: Together, these data suggest that myosin activity is relatively low in the early embryo.
evidence: This is inferred from simulation results and in vivo observations, and supported by citations to studies showing inhibitors of myosin activity are required for maintaining proper syncytial architecture.

claim: Several inhibitors of myosin activity are required for maintaining proper syncytial architecture of the early Drosophila embryo.
source: Indeed, several inhibitors of myosin activity are required for maintaining proper syncytial architecture of the early Drosophila embryo (Lee and Harris, 2013; Mason et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018), and a specific mechanism locally elevates myosin activity for budding and full division of mono-nucleated primordial germ cells from the syncytium (Cinalli and Lehmann, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lee and Harris, 2013; Mason et al., 2016; and Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: A specific mechanism locally elevates myosin activity for budding and full division of mono-nucleated primordial germ cells from the syncytium.
source: Indeed, several inhibitors of myosin activity are required for maintaining proper syncytial architecture of the early Drosophila embryo (Lee and Harris, 2013; Mason et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018), and a specific mechanism locally elevates myosin activity for budding and full division of mono-nucleated primordial germ cells from the syncytium (Cinalli and Lehmann, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cinalli and Lehmann, 2013.

claim: In simulations, centrifugal cap growth with weakly contractile actomyosin networks (0.1 activity) resulted in improved local smoothness but the network-network interface was wavy, and each clearance gained a hexagon-like shape.
source: Compared with the myosin network boundaries formed in the absence of Arp2/3 networks (Figure 3C–D), local smoothness improved but the network-network interface was wavy, and each clearance gained a hexagon-like shape (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Sensitivity analyses showed a failure to form a smooth and circular interface over a wide range of parameter values affecting the myosin network, the Arp2/3 network, and their interface.
source: Sensitivity analyses showed a failure to form a smooth and circular interface over a wide range of parameter values affecting the myosin network, the Arp2/3 network, and their interface (Figure 4—figure supplements 1–6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sensitivity analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 1–6.

claim: In simulations, Arp2/3 network growth induced an aggregation of myosin nodes at the interface.
source: However, Arp2/3 network growth did induce an aggregation of myosin nodes at the interface (Figure 4A, arrows).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In simulations, myosin node connections became substantially longer than their resting length specifically at the interface, and only with Arp2/3 network growth.
source: Also, myosin node connections became substantially longer than their resting length specifically at the interface, and only with Arp2/3 network growth (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In the presence of growing Arp2/3 networks, node-node connections of two or more pixels greater than resting length rose linearly from 0% of all connections at simulation step 0, to 0.48 ± 0.01% at step 500, to 2.05 ± 0.06% at step 2500.
source: In the presence of growing Arp2/3 networks, node-node connections of two or more pixels greater than resting length rose linearly from 0% of all connections at simulation step 0, to 0.48 ± 0.01% at step 500, to 2.05 ± 0.06% at step 2500 (calculated from four simulations with distinct starting distributions, a myosin node density of 0.2, and a myosin node activity of 0.1; p<0.001 comparing steps 500 and 2500).
evidence: This is calculated from simulation data with statistical analysis.

claim: In the absence of growing caps, the percentages of stretched connections remained at <0.003% from simulation steps 0 to 2500.
source: In the absence of growing caps, the percentages remained at <0.003% from simulation steps 0 to 2500.
evidence: This is calculated from simulation data.

claim: Arp2/3 network growth aggregated myosin nodes at the interface and increased tension between myosin nodes at the interface.
source: Thus, Arp2/3 network growth aggregated myosin nodes at the interface and increased tension between myosin nodes at the interface.
evidence: This is concluded from simulation data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: In vivo imaging revealed an Arp2/3-dependent accumulation of myosin at the smooth and circular interface between each cap and myosin border.
source: Although proper syncytial structure requires regulators that reduce cortical actomyosin activity (Lee and Harris, 2013; Mason et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018), our in vivo imaging revealed an Arp2/3-dependent accumulation of myosin at the smooth and circular interface between each cap and myosin border (Figure 3A, black arrows).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Mechanical enhancement of actomyosin activity is evident in vivo.
source: Mechanical enhancement of actomyosin activity is evident in vivo (Effler et al., 2006; Fernandez-Gonzalez et al., 2009), and implicated mechanisms include stabilization of the myosin-actin interaction (Kobb et al., 2017; Kovács et al., 2007; Yamashiro et al., 2018), and alignment of actin filaments for optimal myosin activity (Ennomani et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Effler et al., 2006 and Fernandez-Gonzalez et al., 2009.

claim: Implicated mechanisms for mechanical enhancement of actomyosin activity include stabilization of the myosin-actin interaction.
source: Mechanical enhancement of actomyosin activity is evident in vivo (Effler et al., 2006; Fernandez-Gonzalez et al., 2009), and implicated mechanisms include stabilization of the myosin-actin interaction (Kobb et al., 2017; Kovács et al., 2007; Yamashiro et al., 2018), and alignment of actin filaments for optimal myosin activity (Ennomani et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kobb et al., 2017; Kovács et al., 2007; and Yamashiro et al., 2018.

claim: Implicated mechanisms for mechanical enhancement of actomyosin activity include alignment of actin filaments for optimal myosin activity.
source: Mechanical enhancement of actomyosin activity is evident in vivo (Effler et al., 2006; Fernandez-Gonzalez et al., 2009), and implicated mechanisms include stabilization of the myosin-actin interaction (Kobb et al., 2017; Kovács et al., 2007; Yamashiro et al., 2018), and alignment of actin filaments for optimal myosin activity (Ennomani et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ennomani et al., 2016.

claim: In simulations, myosin node activity elevation events occurred predominantly at interfaces between the actomyosin and Arp2/3 networks.
source: However, comparison of myosin node activity elevation events with and without Arp2/3 networks revealed that the elevations occurred predominantly at interfaces between the actomyosin and Arp2/3 networks (Figure 4C, arrows), and that they required the Arp2/3 network (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Arp2/3-dependent activations of interface myosin in silico resembled the Arp2/3-dependent accumulations of interface myosin in vivo.
source: These Arp2/3-dependent activations of interface myosin in silico resembled the Arp2/3-dependent accumulations of interface myosin in vivo (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is concluded by comparing simulation data in Figure 4C with in vivo data in Figure 3A.

claim: In simulations, mechanosensitive myosin node activity elevations significantly enhanced the smoothness and circularity of the interfaces.
source: Strikingly, the elevations significantly enhanced the smoothness and circularity of the interfaces (Figure 4D), compared to simulations without the elevations (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 4D compared to Figure 4A.

claim: Quantifications of clearance smoothness, circularity, and area showed the importance of a combination of Arp2/3 network growth and mechanosensitivity of the actomyosin network.
source: Quantifications of clearance smoothness, circularity, and area showed the importance of a combination of Arp2/3 network growth and mechanosensitivity of the actomyosin network (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Sensitivity analyses showed that the smooth and circular interfaces arose upon inclusion of mechanosensitivity over a wide range of parameter values affecting the myosin network, the Arp2/3 network, and their interface.
source: Sensitivity analyses showed that the smooth and circular interfaces arose upon inclusion of mechanosensitivity over a wide range of parameter values affecting the myosin network, the Arp2/3 network, and their interface (Figure 4—figure supplements 1–6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sensitivity analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 1–6.

claim: The overall organization of the myosin networks simulated with mechanosensitivity and Arp2/3 network growth closely resembled the myosin networks formed in the presence of Arp2/3 actin caps in wild-type embryos.
source: The overall organization of the myosin networks simulated with mechanosensitivity and Arp2/3 network growth (Figure 4D) closely resembled the myosin networks formed in the presence of Arp2/3 actin caps in wild-type embryos (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is concluded by comparing simulation data in Figure 4D with in vivo data in Figure 3A.

claim: A smooth and circular interface can form from the growth of an Arp2/3 network against a weakly contractile actomyosin network that is mechanosensitive to local activation.
source: These analyses suggest that a smooth and circular interface can form from the growth of an Arp2/3 network against a weakly contractile actomyosin network that is mechanosensitive to local activation.
evidence: This is concluded from simulation data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In simulations of an isolated single ring of myosin nodes with uniform activity, the inner boundary nodes initially moved centrifugally as the ring thinned, and then moved centripetally as the thin and smooth ring constricted.
source: Figure 5A traces the movements of myosin nodes at the inner boundary of the rough ring. Consistent with our single ring analyses in Figure 2E, the inner boundary nodes initially moved centrifugally as the ring thinned (Figure 5A), and then moved centripetally as the thin and smooth ring constricted (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In simulations of an isolated single ring, at the beginning of the simulation, a broad distribution of node displacement angles was observed.
source: At the beginning of the simulation, a broad distribution of node displacement angles was observed (Figure 5C), but during the transition from thinning to constricting, the distribution became biased toward 0° and 180° relative to local radii of the circular network (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In simulations of an isolated single ring, during the transition from thinning to constricting, the distribution of node displacement angles became biased toward 0° and 180° relative to local radii of the circular network.
source: At the beginning of the simulation, a broad distribution of node displacement angles was observed (Figure 5C), but during the transition from thinning to constricting, the distribution became biased toward 0° and 180° relative to local radii of the circular network (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: In simulations of an isolated single ring, nodes mostly displayed back-and-forth displacements closely aligned with the radii during the final stages of the simulation.
source: To understand this bimodal distribution, we examined individual node displacements at full temporal and spatial resolution during the final stages of the simulation. Strikingly, nodes mostly displayed back-and-forth displacements closely aligned with the radii (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The oriented oscillations of nodes provided a signature of contractile actomyosin ring formation in simulations.
source: Although the in vivo relevance of these extremely rapid oscillations is unclear, the oriented oscillations provided a signature of contractile actomyosin ring formation in our simulations.
evidence: This is concluded from simulation data shown in Figure 5.

claim: In two-network simulations, Arp2/3 network growth displaced the myosin nodes centrifugally throughout the simulation, including stages of elevated myosin node activity and when the network-network interface became smooth and circular.
source: Arp2/3 network growth displaced the myosin nodes centrifugally throughout the simulation, including stages of elevated myosin node activity and when the network-network interface became smooth and circular (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: In two-network simulations, initially, a broad distribution of local displacement angles occurred for activated myosin nodes.
source: Initially, a broad distribution of local displacement angles occurred (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: In two-network simulations, the phase of smoothening and circularization was accompanied by a bimodal distribution dominated by angles near 0° and 180° for activated myosin nodes.
source: In contrast, the phase of smoothening and circularization was accompanied by a bimodal distribution dominated by angles near 0° and 180° (Figure 5I–J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 5I-J.

claim: The mechanical elevation of myosin node activity by the pushing forces of Arp2/3 network growth produces a contractile actomyosin ring around the network-network interface.
source: Overall, we conclude that the mechanical elevation of myosin node activity by the pushing forces of Arp2/3 network growth produces a contractile actomyosin ring around the network-network interface, and that contractility of this ring smoothens and circularizes the interface.
evidence: This is concluded from simulation data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Contractility of the actomyosin ring smoothens and circularizes the interface.
source: Overall, we conclude that the mechanical elevation of myosin node activity by the pushing forces of Arp2/3 network growth produces a contractile actomyosin ring around the network-network interface, and that contractility of this ring smoothens and circularizes the interface.
evidence: This is concluded from simulation data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Actomyosin and Arp2/3 networks have been individually simulated as continuum or agent-based models.
source: Actomyosin and Arp2/3 networks have been individually simulated as continuum or agent-based models (Berro, 2018; Cortes et al., 2018; Mogilner and Manhart, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Berro, 2018; Cortes et al., 2018; and Mogilner and Manhart, 2016.

claim: The investigation of roughly distributed elements rearranging into a smooth structure required an agent-based approach.
source: Our investigation of roughly distributed elements rearranging into a smooth structure required an agent-based approach.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological choice based on the research question.

claim: The formation of an extended, smooth interface across a 2D plane is not trivial.
source: The formation of an extended, smooth interface across a 2D plane is not trivial.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle in the Discussion.

claim: Tensile forces can align polymers, but the two ends of the network must be anchored.
source: Tensile forces can align polymers, but the two ends of the network must be anchored.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle based on physical understanding.

claim: A network can anchor to itself, as in the case of a cytokinetic ring.
source: Since a network can anchor to itself, as in the case of a cytokinetic ring (Schwayer et al., 2016), intra-network anchorage may explain the formation of smooth boundaries within a multiply fenestrated myosin network with high contractility (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schwayer et al., 2016 and simulation data in Figure 3C.

claim: Low contractility networks cannot form smooth boundaries on their own.
source: However, low contractility networks cannot form smooth boundaries on their own.
evidence: This is concluded from simulation data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Low contractility is important for maintaining the syncytial state of the early Drosophila embryo.
source: Low contractility is important for maintaining the syncytial state of the early Drosophila embryo (Lee and Harris, 2013; Mason et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018), arrays of podosomes at the base of invasive mammalian cells (Rafiq et al., 2017), and the polar body bud during meiosis II arrest of mouse oocytes (Yi and Li, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lee and Harris, 2013; Mason et al., 2016; and Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: Low contractility is important for arrays of podosomes at the base of invasive mammalian cells.
source: Low contractility is important for maintaining the syncytial state of the early Drosophila embryo (Lee and Harris, 2013; Mason et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018), arrays of podosomes at the base of invasive mammalian cells (Rafiq et al., 2017), and the polar body bud during meiosis II arrest of mouse oocytes (Yi and Li, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rafiq et al., 2017.

claim: Low contractility is important for the polar body bud during meiosis II arrest of mouse oocytes.
source: Low contractility is important for maintaining the syncytial state of the early Drosophila embryo (Lee and Harris, 2013; Mason et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018), arrays of podosomes at the base of invasive mammalian cells (Rafiq et al., 2017), and the polar body bud during meiosis II arrest of mouse oocytes (Yi and Li, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yi and Li, 2012.

claim: Disruptive effects of widespread contractility can be avoided by the local induction of contractility in one material in response to pushing forces from a neighboring material.
source: Our simulations indicate that disruptive effects of widespread contractility can be avoided by the local induction of contractility in one material in response to pushing forces from a neighboring material, and that this induction can produce a contractile ring to smoothen the interface between such materials.
evidence: This is concluded from simulation data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: In the Drosophila embryo, the smooth and circular interface demarcates where the plasma membrane folds to form a dome-like compartment.
source: In the Drosophila embryo, the smooth and circular interface demarcates where the plasma membrane folds to form a dome-like compartment.
evidence: This is stated based on in vivo observations shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Without sufficient growth of the actin cap, the interface remains rough and membrane folding fails.
source: Without sufficient growth of the actin cap, the interface remains rough and membrane folding fails (Figure 3A; Stevenson et al., 2002; Zallen et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo data in Figure 3A and citations to Stevenson et al., 2002 and Zallen et al., 2002.

claim: With weakening of the myosin border, the actin cap grows with an irregular shape and the plasma membrane invagination is lop-sided around the cap.
source: With weakening of the myosin border, the actin cap grows with an irregular shape and the plasma membrane invagination is lop-sided around the cap (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: The simulations show how a smooth and circular structure can emerge from the local interactions of roughly distributed components.
source: Our simulations of network-network interactions at the surface of the early Drosophila embryo show how a smooth and circular structure can emerge from the local interactions of roughly distributed components.
evidence: This is concluded from all simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: This example of refinement by mechanical self-organization is relevant to other cell biological processes, such as mammalian polar body budding and podosome protrusion.
source: This example of refinement by mechanical self-organization is relevant to other cell biological processes, such as mammalian polar body budding (Yi and Li, 2012) and podosome protrusion (van den Dries et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Yi and Li, 2012 and van den Dries et al., 2019.

claim: Refinement by mechanical self-organization is relevant to the refinement of smart materials, including nanocomposites and metamaterials, after an initial printing step.
source: It is also relevant to the refinement of smart materials, including nanocomposites and metamaterials, after an initial printing step (Begley et al., 2019; Holmes, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Begley et al., 2019 and Holmes, 2019.

claim: Biological composite materials can exhibit complex behaviors due to their multiple mechanical properties, and are thus top candidates in advanced manufacturing.
source: Biological composite materials can exhibit complex behaviors due to their multiple mechanical properties, and are thus top candidates in advanced manufacturing (Eder et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Eder et al., 2018 and Wang et al., 2020.

claim: Reconstituted actin networks can be coated with inorganic materials to fabricate specific 3D structures.
source: Notably, reconstituted actin networks can be coated with inorganic materials to fabricate specific 3D structures (Galland et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Galland et al., 2013.

claim: Node-based modelling is applicable to a range of materials, and could identify various roles for mechanical self-organization in device fabrication.
source: Node-based modelling is also applicable to a range of materials, and could identify various roles for mechanical self-organization in device fabrication.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application based on the modeling approach developed in this study.

claim: The cell cortex is 50–400 nm thick.
source: Since the cell cortex is 50–400 nm thick (Chugh and Paluch, 2018; Salbreux et al., 2012; Svitkina, 2020), the positioning of nodes above and below each other in 3D space is represented in the 2D simulation by allowing a maximum of 20 nodes to occupy the same pixel (with no information encoding the third dimension) (see Table 1 for a full list of parameters).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chugh and Paluch, 2018; Salbreux et al., 2012; and Svitkina, 2020.

claim: Myosin mini-filaments have 28–58 motor domains.
source: This design is based on myosin mini-filaments (i) having 28–58 motor domains (Billington et al., 2013; Niederman and Pollard, 1975), which would not all be simultaneous bound to actin (discussed above), (ii) displaying motor domains at angles of up to 180° relative to each other (Billington et al., 2013; Laplante et al., 2016; Niederman and Pollard, 1975; Sellers and Kachar, 1990), and (iii) engaging actin filaments with lengths of ~500 nm for optimal contractility of cortical actomyosin networks (Chugh et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Billington et al., 2013 and Niederman and Pollard, 1975.

claim: Myosin mini-filaments display motor domains at angles of up to 180° relative to each other.
source: This design is based on myosin mini-filaments (i) having 28–58 motor domains (Billington et al., 2013; Niederman and Pollard, 1975), which would not all be simultaneous bound to actin (discussed above), (ii) displaying motor domains at angles of up to 180° relative to each other (Billington et al., 2013; Laplante et al., 2016; Niederman and Pollard, 1975; Sellers and Kachar, 1990), and (iii) engaging actin filaments with lengths of ~500 nm for optimal contractility of cortical actomyosin networks (Chugh et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Billington et al., 2013; Laplante et al., 2016; Niederman and Pollard, 1975; and Sellers and Kachar, 1990.

claim: Myosin mini-filaments engage actin filaments with lengths of ~500 nm for optimal contractility of cortical actomyosin networks.
source: This design is based on myosin mini-filaments (i) having 28–58 motor domains (Billington et al., 2013; Niederman and Pollard, 1975), which would not all be simultaneous bound to actin (discussed above), (ii) displaying motor domains at angles of up to 180° relative to each other (Billington et al., 2013; Laplante et al., 2016; Niederman and Pollard, 1975; Sellers and Kachar, 1990), and (iii) engaging actin filaments with lengths of ~500 nm for optimal contractility of cortical actomyosin networks (Chugh et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chugh et al., 2017.

claim: Cross-linked actin networks display elastic responses to stretching but not compression.
source: In addition, cross-linked actin networks display elastic responses to stretching but not compression (Banerjee et al., 2020; Salbreux et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Banerjee et al., 2020 and Salbreux et al., 2012.

claim: The Arp2/3 complex nucleates actin polymerization.
source: Since the Arp2/3 complex nucleates actin polymerization (Pollard, 2016; Svitkina, 2018) and centrosomes act as spatial landmarks for the induction of Arp2/3-enirched actin caps in Drosophila (Raff and Glover, 1989; Stevenson et al., 2001), an Arp2/3 network is initiated by randomly positioning the nucleation points in a dense inner circle (20 pixel radius with 10% of pixels containing a nucleation point) and a sparse, larger and overlapping circle (50 pixel radius with 1% of pixels containing a nucleation point).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pollard, 2016 and Svitkina, 2018.

claim: The Arp2/3 complex nucleates growth of a new actin polymer at a 70° angle relative to a preexisting polymer.
source: To form a dendritic network, the Arp2/3 complex nucleates growth of a new actin polymer at a 70° angle relative to a preexisting polymer (Pollard, 2016; Svitkina, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pollard, 2016 and Svitkina, 2018.

claim: In vitro, branching can occur from either side of the mother filament, anywhere along the mother filament (with a preference toward the barbed end), and the mother and daughter filaments polymerize at the same rate.
source: In vitro, branching can occur from either side of the mother filament, anywhere along the mother filament (with a preference toward the barbed end), and the mother and daughter filaments polymerize at the same rate (Amann and Pollard, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Amann and Pollard, 2001.

claim: Capping of actin plus ends promotes shorter filament lengths that resist buckling and exert more effective pushing forces.
source: Capping of actin plus ends promotes shorter filament lengths that resist buckling and exert more effective pushing forces, whereas depolymerization of older filaments by actin depolymerization factors allows network turnover (Banerjee et al., 2020; Pollard, 2016; Pollard and Borisy, 2003; Svitkina, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Banerjee et al., 2020; Pollard, 2016; Pollard and Borisy, 2003; and Svitkina, 2018.

claim: Depolymerization of older filaments by actin depolymerization factors allows network turnover.
source: Capping of actin plus ends promotes shorter filament lengths that resist buckling and exert more effective pushing forces, whereas depolymerization of older filaments by actin depolymerization factors allows network turnover (Banerjee et al., 2020; Pollard, 2016; Pollard and Borisy, 2003; Svitkina, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Banerjee et al., 2020; Pollard, 2016; Pollard and Borisy, 2003; and Svitkina, 2018.
